title: HarborPoint - tokenburst & architectural discovery
summary: Discovery focused on p95 streaming latency targets and burst token throughput. HarborPoint runs a hybrid inference stack and needs guidance on hosted vs dedicated vs private for a new real-time summarization feature. Discussed concurrency, KV/prefix caching, fallback model variants, and security controls. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot and exchange prompt sets and sample traces.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-01-08 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Omar Malik, Priya Sinha (Redwood); Alex Park, Laura Nguyen, Ben Torres, Samira Khan (HarborPoint)

Summary (auto): HarborPoint has a streaming summarization product embedded in their desktop client. They expect bursts of activity during market opens with short sessions that require low p95 latency for streaming tokens and high token/sec during bursts. They asked about whether Redwood hosted can meet p95 targets or if Dedicated/Private is required, plus security/compliance questions.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, we're Maya (AE), Omar (SE), Priya on the call. how's HarborPoint doing?
[00:12] Alex Park: Good, thanks. we're calling because we're evaluating inference options for a new live summarization feature across our trading desktop. low latency during open and token bursts are the big concern.
[00:24] Laura Nguyen: And we have some constraints — company policy requires SOC2, SSO/SAML, and for certain markets they want data residency controls. We want to understand hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs.
[00:37] Maya Chen: Totally makes sense. Can you share your rough p95 target and concurrency profile?
[00:44] Ben Torres: We're aiming for p95 end-to-end streaming latency of like 80 ms to 150 ms when clients stream. Typical prompt is 60-120 tokens, with a median response length of 80 tokens. Burst conditions at open cause token/sec leverage — peak aggregate is ~18k tokens/sec across the cluster, sustained off-peak is around 1.2k.
[01:08] Omar Malik: Okay so two dimensions — low p95 per session for streaming and very high aggregate token burst. Are those numbers for single region?
[01:16] Alex Park: Yes, primarily NA-east but we also need EU fallback. We're open to routing policies.
[01:22] Priya Sinha: Quick clarifying Q: when you say p95 80-150 ms, is that server-only, or client-perceived end-to-end?
[01:28] Ben Torres: Client-perceived. From when the first chunk of streaming text starts arriving. So network plus server.
[01:33] Maya Chen: Got it. For hosted Redwood API, achievable p95 depends on model choice, sequence length, and streaming chunk size. For smaller models and optimized serving runtime we often see p95 streaming start times in the 50-120 ms range for regional requests, but bursts can change that.
[01:48] Samira Khan: What about tail latency during CPU noise or noisy neighbors? we need guarantees.
[01:53] Omar Malik: That's where Dedicated and Private come in. Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput; you get much tighter p95 guarantees because you're not competing for capacity. Private (VPC or on-prem) gives you full isolation plus KMS integrations for keys. Hosted can be sufficient if you plan fallbacks and autoscaling policies — but for strict SLA-backed p95 you'd typically look at Dedicated.
[02:15] Laura Nguyen: For cost reasons we were hoping hosted would work. Do you have numbers for token/sec per GPU in dedicated?
[02:23] Priya Sinha: It depends on model size and quantization. e.g., for a 7B quantized variant on an A100-ish node you might get 3-4k tokens/sec sustained per worker for streaming workloads; an 70B large fp16 model is much lower. But again the runtime uses continuous batching and kernel selection — we'll recommend configs per your prompt distribution.
[02:44] Alex Park: So to hit 18k peak, we'd need around 5 to 6 workers assuming 3.5k tokens/sec each, plus headroom?
[02:53] Omar Malik: Correct, plus concurrency management, prefix caching, and burst autoscale buffer. Also beware of session-affinity if you want low per-session p95 in streaming — binding the session to a warm KV-cache-enabled worker helps.
[03:07] Ben Torres: What's the KV/prefix cache behavior? our docs mention heavy reuse of system prompt and user context.
[03:14] Priya Sinha: Redwood runtime supports KV cache and prefix caching; for repeated prompt prefixes (like system prompt + user metadata) you get near-zero recompute for cached tokens. That reduces per-token compute in early steps, which helps p95. But cache hit rates depend on request variety — for desktop clients with similar system prompts, hit rates should be high.
[03:31] Alex Park: That would be huge; a 30-40% reduction in compute during the start of a stream would lower p95 a lot.
[03:37] Maya Chen: Right. Also for hosted we expose guidance and will run a warmup plan to populate prefix caches during the pilot.
[03:45] [00:03:50] Customer (generic): um hmm, sorry brief interruption — network hiccup.
[03:51] Laura Nguyen: Another question — how do fallbacks work if capacity is constrained? we need graceful degradation not 500s.
[03:58] Omar Malik: We have policy routing — you can configure fallbacks to a cheaper/quantized model or to a lower concurrency lane. For streaming we can fall back to coarser chunk sizes to maintain throughput. For crucial SLAs you can also mix Hosted with Dedicated: route most requests to Dedicated and overflow to Hosted as a safety net. That gives predictable capacity plus burst headroom.
[04:22] Alex Park: Does overflow to hosted leak any data? we need to avoid sending PII to shared environments.
[04:28] Samira Khan: Exactly, data leakage concerns.
[04:31] Priya Sinha: We support data tagging and configurable retention. For Hosted you can mark requests as no-retain, and we have enterprise isolation features and contractual controls. But if your legal/regulatory teams require no shared-hosted fallback, then Dedicated with Reserved capacity or Private is the safer bet.
[04:48] Ben Torres: For Private deployments — what's the operational overhead? we run Kafka + k8s already.
[04:54] Omar Malik: Private (VPC or on-prem) includes a customer-managed data plane; Redwood provides the control plane and packaging for the runtime. On-prem will need GPU provisioning, container runtime, and some infra work for autoscaling. We provide deployment docs and a runbook. For teams with existing infra it's typically 4-8 weeks to stand up.
[05:09] Alex Park: Good to know. And cost-wise, Dedicated seems cheaper per-token than hosted at scale?
[05:15] Priya Sinha: Generally yes once you amortize committed capacity. Hosted is flexible but unit cost is typically higher; Dedicated with reserved nodes and optimized quantization can lower unit costs materially. Our Optimize tool can simulate your monthly token profile and recommend a commit size.
[05:31] [00:05:31] Customer side murmur — someone typing
[05:36] Maya Chen: Quick technical check — can you share a representative request trace? the shape of token generation (burst vs steady streaming) influences our kernel selection.
[05:45] Alex Park: We'll share traces. We have a sample where the first 20 tokens are system and meta, then incremental user messages.
[05:51] Omar Malik: Perfect. On the p95 discussion: we usually break p95 into two metrics — time-to-first-chunk (how quickly the first tokens arrive) and steady-state token latency (per-token compute). For interactive streaming the time-to-first-chunk is most visible. Caching and warm workers improve that.
[06:10] Ben Torres: About concurrency — we expect a lot of short-lived websocket sessions. How do you manage worker saturation? is pre-warming possible?
[06:18] Priya Sinha: Yes, we have warm pools and autoscale policies tuned for connection churn. You can set minimum worker counts, pre-warm policies before market opens (cron-based scaling), and per-route concurrency caps. That avoids cold starts and noisy neighbor spikes.
[06:33] Laura Nguyen: How deterministic are p95 guarantees across days? we want to avoid surprises around market open.
[06:39] Omar Malik: With Dedicated plus committed burst capacity you can get SLA-backed p95 windows. For Hosted, p95 averages are usually stable, but extreme bursts can increase tails; again fallback and autoscale policies mitigate that.
[06:52] Alex Park: Can we run a token/sec benchmark with our traces? say a synthetic replay to measure throughput per worker.
[06:58] Maya Chen: Absolutely. We can run a benchmark using your anonymized traces against a matrix of model variants and quantization configs to estimate tokens/sec and p95. We'll also measure streaming start latency under concurrency.
[07:12] Ben Torres: what's typical observed p95 for time-to-first-chunk on an optimized 7B quantized model in a single region under low concurrency?
[07:19] Omar Malik: On a good warm worker you might see 40-80 ms to first chunk depending on networking. With caching and small chunk sizes it's closer to the low end. But if you have cold workers or heavy batching windows, it can rise above 150 ms.
[07:33] Samira Khan: Security quick Q — do you support customer-managed KMS for encryption of request data at rest in Dedicated?
[07:39] Priya Sinha: Yes, Dedicated and Private both integrate with customer KMS/HSM. Hosted also supports enterprise KMS integrations for keys used in logs/retention features.
[07:50] Alex Park: For the pilot, we want to test both hosted (for overflow) and a small Dedicated pool to compare. Is that something Redwood can provision quickly?
[07:58] Maya Chen: Yes, we can put together a two-arm pilot: small Dedicated reserved pool sized to your expected sustained baseline plus Hosted overflow for peak bursts. We'll run token/sec benchmarks and a streaming p95 pass.
[08:09] Laura Nguyen: Any guidance on chunk sizes? smaller chunks reduce first-chunk latency but increase overhead.
[08:16] Omar Malik: Exactly. There's a trade-off: very small chunks (~8-16 tokens) reduce initial perceived latency but increase framing overhead and network roundtrips. We recommend testing 16-32 token chunk sizes for your client with our runtime — often a sweet spot. We'll measure both in the pilot.
[08:32] Ben Torres: About observability — can we get per-route token/latency breakdowns and token-level cost data?
[08:38] Priya Sinha: Yes, Redwood Console exposes per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost, p95 latency by route, and traces. For pilots we can extend retention temporarily to capture detailed metrics.
[08:51] [00:08:51] brief pause as someone pulls up a doc
[08:56] Alex Park: For network hiccups, do you recommend client-side buffering?
[09:00] Maya Chen: Yes, client buffering with jitter tolerance is common. Also server chunking and idempotency keys to allow retries without duplication. We'll share best practices.
[09:10] Laura Nguyen: One more — license / procurement timeline. We're budgeting for Q1 rollout. Can procurement approve pilot spend quickly?
[09:18] Maya Chen: We typically do a one-off pilot agreement; I can send a template. If procurement needs SOW or security annex, we can attach SOC2/ISO docs.
[09:26] Samira Khan: We'll want a security questionnaire filled out — do you have an existing security pack?
[09:30] Priya Sinha: Yes, we'll share our security pack (SOC2 attestation, encryption docs, data flow diagrams).
[09:36] Alex Park: What about model version pinning and rollouts? we need stable model behavior in prod.
[09:42] Omar Malik: Redwood supports model pinning per-route and rollout policies (canary, A/B). For pilot we can pin a stable quantized variant. Also quality monitoring to detect regression against your eval set.
[09:54] Ben Torres: For on-prem private, we'd need to validate that your runtime supports our GPU infra. Which GPUs are supported?
[09:59] Priya Sinha: We support common GPUs (A100, H100, RTX-8xxx series) and have hardware-abstracted kernel choices. We'll ask for system details as part of the pilot.
[10:11] Alex Park: Ok let's recap then next steps.
[10:15] Maya Chen: Recap: Redwood to propose a 2-week pilot with two arms: (1) small Dedicated reserved pool sized for baseline sustained tokens/sec, (2) Hosted overflow configured with no-retain tagging for non-sensitive routes. We'll run token/sec benchmarks replaying your traces across a matrix (7B quantized, 13B q4, and a 70B fp16 variant) and measure time-to-first-chunk and steady-state token latency. Redwood to share pricing matrix, pilot SOW, and security pack. HarborPoint to share anonymized traces, prompt sets, traffic histograms, and procurement contacts.
[10:41] Alex Park: Sounds good. Ben will be our lead on benching, Laura will handle infra. Samira will handle security questions.
[10:50] Maya Chen: Great. We'll send the pilot docs and benchmark plan. Any final quick Qs?
[10:55] [00:10:55] Ben Torres: Just one — can you include a quick note on expected costs for the 2-week pilot run?
[11:02] Priya Sinha: We'll include an estimate in the pilot SOW — ballpark compute + bandwidth + reserved node pricing.
[11:08] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the docs.
[11:11] Alex Park: Thanks. bye.

End of transcript.
notes: Pilot will include two-arm test: Dedicated baseline + Hosted overflow
HarborPoint must provide anonymized request traces and prompt sets
Redwood will run token/sec benchmarks and streaming p95 measurements
